scenes.tts: In Mozambique's Gorongosa National Park, soldiers on both sides of a civil war killed elephants for ivory. The war lasted from nineteen seventy-seven to nineteen ninety-two. Before the war, about one in five sampled females had no tusks. Among the females that survived, about half had none. The rise did not come from elephants losing their tusks. So how did the population change?

scenes.tts: The answer starts with a fact. Individuals differ. Variation means the differences among individuals in a population. An allele is one version of a gene. A mutation is a change in DNA. It is the original source of new alleles. Gene flow is the movement of alleles from one population to another. Sexual reproduction shuffles alleles that already exist into new combinations.
scenes.visual: Row of different individuals; a box of allele squares; a new square appears (mutation); squares arrive from a second box (gene flow); squares regroup in pairs.

Sexual reproduction shuffles alleles that already exist into new combinations.

scenes.tts: Populations tend to make more young than the environment can support. A female blue crab in the Chesapeake Bay may carry an egg mass of about seven hundred fifty thousand to eight million eggs. Only a small fraction become adult crabs. Most die young. An elephant usually has one calf at a birth.

scenes.tts: Now add a pressure. A selective pressure is anything in the environment that makes some variants more likely to survive or reproduce than others. In Gorongosa, poachers wanted ivory. So tusked elephants were killed more often. Tuskless females already existed, and they survived more often. That is natural selection. Individuals with certain inherited variations survive and reproduce more than others.
scenes.visual: 40 tokens; poaching arrow; most tusked tokens removed, one tuskless removed.
scenes.narration: Now add a pressure. A selective pressure is anything in the environment that makes some variants more likely to survive or reproduce than others. In Gorongosa, poachers wanted ivory. So tusked elephants were killed more often. Tuskless females already existed, and they survived more often. That is natural selection. Individuals with certain inherited variations survive and reproduce more than others.

scenes.tts: Now count the survivors. The share of females with no tusks went up. Tuskless survivors left more of the next generation. So that inherited variation becomes more common in later generations. No single elephant changed. The population changed. Individuals do not evolve. Populations do.
scenes.visual: Survivors beside two share bars: before about 1 in 5, survivors about half; one unchanged elephant; individuals versus populations.
scenes.narration: Now count the survivors. The share of females with no tusks went up. Tuskless survivors left more of the next generation. So that inherited variation becomes more common in later generations. No single elephant changed. The population changed. Individuals do not evolve. Populations do.

scenes.tts: Back to the question. Why do some individuals survive and reproduce while others do not? Because they differ, and some variations suit the conditions better. Those individuals leave more young. So those variations become more common. A strong pressure, like heavy poaching, can change a trait within a few decades. A weak pressure changes it slowly. Remember this rule. Individuals differ, some survive more, and the population changes.
